toc.title: Shutdown and freeze are different things
What coming out of shutdown looks like
Why it can feel like freeze

blocks.p: What if you're coming out of shutdown and you find yourself in a new stuck state, a new predicament, which is having more freeze activation? A viewer asked me this on YouTube:

q: Since I discovered you, I was able to get out of shutdown mode that I've been in for years. Maybe most of my life. But now I'm in freeze. And while I understand slightly touching on a safe state, I'm not sure I understand what touching on defense feels like. Can you please explain that for me again?

blocks.p: First, congratulations on the progress. I'm really happy to read that. Let's learn, or relearn, what shutdown and freeze are. Then I'll address in general what could be happening when someone goes through this. I don't know about this person in particular. And then I'll cover how to lightly touch upon defensive activation.

blocks.h: Shutdown and freeze are different things

blocks.p: In the Polyvagal Theory, shutdown is a state of limp collapse. It is the last resort when we cannot be safe, run away, or be aggressive. If none of those strategies work, if we're not able to be safe and can't run away or fight off a danger, then we collapse. We shut down. Our body plays dead.

Freeze is, just like shutdown, immobilization, but it's a tense immobilization, more like a statue. The body is ready to run away or fight, but also immobilizing at the same time. Freeze is a combination of flight or fight plus shutdown. Both of these polyvagal autonomic states are occurring at the same time. We have our foot on the gas and on the brake at the same time.
Shutdown is not a mixed state like that. Shutdown is a primary state. The dorsal vagal pathways are active, or overly active, and someone goes into a limp collapse.
So to sum it up: shutdown is a limp, collapsed immobilization, and freeze is a tense immobilization. They're similar, but different, and that difference plays into what could be happening here.

blocks.h: What coming out of shutdown looks like

blocks.p: Prolonged shutdown, even decades of living in it, is not playing dead. But the body is in a state of collapse. It's in a state of disconnection, numbness, and low energy, unable to fulfill the wants the person has. They want to do things, but they lack the energy to make it happen. The shutdown activation is active in the system for decades, and that's what it can look like day to day.

To get to shutdown, someone can't be in their safety state, they can't run away, they can't fight, and so the body collapses. One can get stuck in a state of defense, and one of those states of defense is shutdown. That's trauma.

To come out of that stuck, traumatized shutdown state, you have to do the reverse. You can't just be done with shutdown and then feel safe and fulfilled and know how to live a content life. That's not exactly how it works. For really full healing, you have to go from shutdown, through fight, through flight, and then back into your safety state.

That's the very one-dimensional, cartoon way of looking at it. It's more complex than that. All of these states are active within us pretty much at all times. Right now I'm sitting still, so I'm immobile. But my hands are moving, and I'm talking a lot and thinking critically and rapidly. So I'm in my safety state, but I'm also kind of mobile, and also immobile. All these things are happening at once. One's dominant state might be shutdown, or flight and fight, or safety.

If your dominant state is shutdown, then for it to ease up, you have to have more access to safety. You have to build up the strength of your safety state. As you do that, the dominance of shutdown eases, but now flight and fight come more online, because our body has to go through those autonomic shifts to get even deeper into its safety state and have more of a dominant safety state.
Irene Lyon described the same thing about depression when she was on the podcast:

q: To come out of [depression]... you have to rev the system up again. You have to get it comfortable with feeling energy.

blocks.h: Why it can feel like freeze

blocks.p: As you come out of shutdown, there's more sympathetic flight and fight activation, probably specifically fight. But it's not all at once. It's not like you're in shutdown now, and twelve hours from now, at the end of the day, you're out of shutdown. It's a gradual process. As immobilization softens, mobilization increases, but it's not one or the other.

So you might have a ton of shutdown now, and two months from now, that shutdown has decreased by 50%. Let's give it a number. Since it's decreased by 50%, now the mobilization system has increased by, I don't know, 10%, and safety has increased by 40%. I'm making up numbers. Don't worry about the numbers.

Even though shutdown has gone down and safety has come up, there's now more room in your system for sympathetic activation. But the shutdown is still there. So, especially if there's not enough safety in the system, as shutdown recedes, sympathetic comes up, and now we have sympathetic flight and fight and shutdown co-occurring.

That could be the process of healing. It could be a sign of progress. It's not "the shutdown's done and I'm good." It's "Shutdown is less, cool. And now I also have to feel and use my newfound sympathetic fight activation, plus seek out safety and practice feeling that." There's a lot happening all at once.

With shutdown less and sympathetic more, both of those are in the system, and it could feel like a freeze. Probably not a full-on freeze. It could feel like there's something I'm working on, and I'm making progress on it, but I keep stalling. Or there's something I want to achieve, and I'm just not moving forward with it. I want to create this art project, and I started it, but now I just sit there staring at the canvas. The body wants to do something, but it stalls, or kind of freezes.

It's not an intense freeze where your muscles are actually tense and your eyes are wide. It's not a panic attack. Could it look like a panic attack? Could it look like a freeze? Eh, kind of. In my client work, and for myself, as shutdown recedes there's definitely more sympathetic in the system, and there's no one way it looks:

ul: A big burst of it: "Oh, this feels great, let me just run with this and use it." But it's all over the place, so it's dysregulated.
Out-of-control sympathetic. Not hurting someone, but a lot of aggression in my system, and now I'm telling people off.
Getting a ton of work done, but not really being that productive. Just spinning my wheels.

blocks.p: So when we come out of shutdown and notice some lingering or background freeze, what could be happening is that now there's more sympathetic, but there's also still shutdown, and those two things are in a sense competing. In your safety state, the strength is lacking to allow both of those activations: to allow yourself to be shut down, but also to move over to mobilization.

The safety state always needs to be strengthened. All of us, I think, should be working on that every day. As the safety state strengthens, shutdown will continue to recede, and your safety state will be able to greet and welcome the emerging sympathetic activation and point it in a direction that's meaningful. Toward goals, hobbies, productivity, exercise, whatever you want. The direction that's right for you.

The question was: I know how to touch upon safety, but how do I touch upon defense? The way I break it down, the process is very similar for both. Can you mindfully connect with what you feel in the present moment, no matter what it is? That's not easy.

Here's what it looks like with safety. Say you go for a walk, and it's a sunny day, and you like that feeling. "Yay, this is nice." That's safety, and that's nice, but it's passive safety. You're not really mindfully connecting with it, so you're not getting the most out of it.
The next step is to mindfully experience what it's like to go out for a walk on a sunny day:

ul: Can you notice how the sun feels on your skin, and how that affects your breath?
Can you notice what the chill of the air feels like on your face, and how you feel about that internally? What happens inside of you based on that external input?
Can you listen to a bird and notice whether you like it or not? If you like it, how could you tell? What do you feel internally? Are you more or less likely to smile when you listen to that bird?

blocks.p: When we mindfully attune to these one by one and notice how we feel inside of it, that, to me, is mindfulness. That's mindfully putting the reps in and feeling your safety state when it's there.
It's the same thing with defensive activation: can we notice it when it's there and mindfully connect with it?

ol: Anchor in safety first. Starting out, I encourage people to have an environment in their home that gives them consistent cues of safety. I call it the passive safety environment, and I write about it in [Book 2, Building Safety](piece:anchor-environment). It has the right sound, the right lighting, the right scents, the right seating, whatever that is for you as an individual. In it, you feel your safety state and mindfully connect with it. Then ask: what else is inside of me?

Get curious about the defense. Once you're grounded in safety, you can lightly touch upon defensive activation, or deeply if you want to. "I know I have a chronic shutdown," or "I know I have this lingering freeze happening within me. I'm in my safety state. I'm connected to my passive safety environment. I feel present. I feel connected. I'm curious and interested in what the world is like inside of me. So what does this shutdown feel like? What does it truly feel like to experience numbness? What does frustration feel like?"
Permit it. First off, give those feelings permission to be.
Find where it lives in your body. Where do I feel shutdown? Where do I feel frustration?

Spend some time with it and describe it. If you can identify where it lives, notice it. What does it look like? If I touched it, what would it feel like? What shape is it? What size? What color? I know these are weird questions, but this is how we connect with our internal world: through description. Initially you might have to be very objective and ask yourself those questions. It gets easier over time, and eventually you don't have to.

blocks.p: If you just stuck with "It's okay for me to feel shut down," or "It's okay for me to feel a little bit of frustration," and noticed where it lives in your body while staying anchored in your safety state, I would call that a light practice.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: As you go deeper, you actually feel into and notice the experience of whatever emotion or state you're allowing. That's where real change and unstucking can happen. We can allow frustration, or that emerging sympathetic activation, maybe anxiety, to be present and connect with it mindfully. Then we pendulate over to our safety state and reconnect with that, and then pendulate back and forth. That is what truly allows the next step of unstucking.

But lightly? Be anchored in your safety state, in your passive safety environment, and then be mindful and curious about what else is inside of you, and what that lingering defensive activation feels like. That's how you lightly touch upon it.
